Question 1¶

ISLP chapter 7 exercise #1

It was mentioned in this chapter that a cubic regression spline with one knot at $\xi$ can be obtained using a basis of the form $x,\ x^2,\ x^3,\ (x - \xi)^3_+$, where $(x - \xi)^3_+ = (x - \xi)^3$ if $(x > \xi)$ and equals 0 otherwise. We will now show that a function of the form $$f(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \beta_3 x^3 + \beta_4 (x - \xi)^3_+$$ is indeed a cubic regression spline, regardless of the values of $\beta_0, \beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3, \beta_4$.

(a) Find a cubic polynomial $$ f_1(x) = a_1 + b_1 x + c_1 x^2 + d_1 x^3 $$ such that $f(x) = f_1(x)$ for all $x \leq \xi$. Express $a_1, b_1, c_1, d_1$ in terms of $\beta_0, \beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3, \beta_4$.

$$ \begin{align*} a_1=\beta_0 \\ b_1=\beta_1 \\ c_1=\beta_2 \\ d_1=\beta_3 \end{align*} $$

(b) Find a cubic polynomial $$ f_2(x) = a_2 + b_2 x + c_2 x^2 + d_2 x^3 $$ such that $f(x) = f_2(x)$ for all $x > \xi$. Express $a_2, b_2, c_2, d_2$ in terms of $\beta_0, \beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3, \beta_4$.

$$ \begin{align*} a_2 &= \beta_0-\beta_4\xi^3 \\ b_2 &= \beta_1+3\beta_4\xi^2 \\ c_2 &= \beta_2-3\beta_4\xi \\ d_2 &= \beta_3+\beta_4 \end{align*} $$

(c) Show that $f_1(\xi) = f_2(\xi)$. That is, $f(x)$ is continuous at $\xi$.

$$ \begin{align*} f_1(\xi) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1\xi + \beta_2\xi^2 + \beta_3\xi^3 \\ f_2(\xi) &= \beta_0-\beta_4\xi^3 + (\beta_1+3\beta_4\xi^2)\xi + (\beta_2-3\beta_4\xi)\xi^2 + (\beta_3+\beta_4)\xi^3 \\ &= \beta_0 + \beta_1\xi + \beta_2\xi^2 + \beta_3\xi^3 \end{align*} $$

That is $f(x)$ is continous at $\xi$

(d) Show that $f'_1(\xi) = f'_2(\xi)$. That is, $f'(x)$ is continuous at $\xi$.

$$ \begin{align*} f'_1(\xi) &= \beta_1 + 2\beta_2\xi + 3\beta_3\xi^2 \\ f'_2(\xi) &= (\beta_1+3\beta_4\xi^2) + 2(\beta_2-3\beta_4\xi)\xi + 3(\beta_3+\beta_4)\xi^2 \\ &= \beta_1 + 2\beta_2\xi + 3\beta_3\xi^2 \end{align*} $$

That is, $f'(x)$ is continuous at $\xi$

(e) Show that $f''_1(\xi) = f''_2(\xi)$. That is, $f''(x)$ is continuous at $\xi$

$$ \begin{align*} f''_1(\xi) &= 2\beta_2 + 6\beta_3\xi \\ f''_2(\xi) &= 2(\beta_2-3\beta_4\xi) + 6(\beta_3+\beta_4)\xi \\ &= 2\beta_2 + 6\beta_3\xi \end{align*} $$

That is, $f''(x)$ is continuous at $\xi$

Question 2¶

ISLP chapter 7 exercise #2. For this problem, there are two important points to consider:

  • Each part of the problem requires you to create a “sketch.” By sketch, we mean an actual drawing. This could be a photograph of something you have hand-drawn on paper or an image created using a digital drawing tool. While creating a plot with matplotlib is also an option, it might require more effort than necessary for this task. The sketches don’t need to be perfect, but should include a vertical axis, a horizontal axis, at least six points that represent plausible training data, and a basic illustration of the curve $\hat{g}$.
  • Regarding part (e) of the problem, which looks at the scenario when $λ= 0$ and $m = 3$. In this scenario, the curve $\hat{g}$ is not uniquely defined; there are many different answers that will all be considered correct. However, this doesn’t mean that any sketch will be considered correct.

Suppose that a curve $\hat{g}$ is computed to smoothly fit a set of (n) points using the following formula: $$ \hat{g} = \arg\min_{g}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - g(x_i))^2 + \lambda \int\left[g^{(m)}(x)\right]^2 dx\right), $$ where $g^{(m)}$ represents the $m$th derivative of $g$ (and $g^{(0)} = g$). Provide example sketches of $\hat{g}$ in each of the following scenarios.

Question 3¶

ISLP chapter 7 exercise #3. This requires another sketch. As before, a drawing is what we’re looking for. However, for this sketch, as per the instructions in the textbook problem, it must include annotations detailing “intercepts, slopes, and other relevant information.” More specifically, the sketch should clearly show:

  • The horizontal and vertical axes of the plot.
  • The point where the curve crosses the $y$-axis.
  • The point(s) where the curve intersects the $x$-axis, if any, within the range of $x$ values being sketched.
  • The slope of any straight segments of the curve.

Suppose we fit a curve with basis functions
$b_1(X) = X,\ b_2(X) = (X - 1)^2 I(X \geq 1). $ (Note that $I(X \geq 1)$ equals 1 for $X \geq 1$ and 0 otherwise.)
We fit the linear regression model
$$ Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 b_1(X) + \beta_2 b_2(X) + \epsilon, $$
and obtain coefficient estimates $\hat{\beta}_0 = 1, \quad \hat{\beta}_1 = 1, \quad \hat{\beta}_2 = -2.$ Sketch the estimated curve between $X = -2$and $X = 2.$ Note the intercepts, slopes, and other relevant information.

$$ \begin{align*} \hat{Y} &= \beta_0 + \hat{\beta}_1b_1(X) + \hat{\beta}_2b_2(X) \\ &= 1 + X -2(X-1)^2I(X\ge1) \\ &= \begin{cases} X+1, & X<1 \\ -2X^2+5X-1, & X\ge1 \end{cases} \end{align*} $$

Question 4¶

ISLP chapter 7 exercise #4 (cf. remarks for the previous problem)

Suppose we fit a curve with a basis functions $ b_1(X) = I(0 \leq X \leq 2) - (X - 1)I(1 \leq X \leq 2),\ b_2(X) = (X - 3)I(3 \leq X \leq 4) + I(4 < X \leq 5). $We fit the linear regression model
$$ Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 b_1(X) + \beta_2 b_2(X) + \epsilon, $$
and obtain coefficient estimates $\hat{\beta}_0 = 1, \hat{\beta}_1 = 1, \hat{\beta}_2 = 3.$ Sketch the estimated curve between $X = -2$ and $X = 6.$ Note the intercepts, slopes, and other relevant information.

$$ \begin{align*} \hat{Y} &= \hat{\beta_0} + \hat{\beta_1}b_1(X) + \hat{\beta_2}(X) \\[1mm] &= 1 + I(0 \leq X \leq 2) - (X - 1)I(1 \leq X \leq 2) + 3(X - 3)I(3 \leq X \leq 4) + 3I(4 < X \leq 5) \\[1mm] &= \begin{cases} 1 & X<0 \\ 2 & 0\le X < 1 \\ 3-X & 1\le X \le 2 \\ 1 & 2<X<3 \\ 3X-8 & 3\le X \le4 \\ 4 & 4<X\le5\\ 1 & X>5 \end{cases} \end{align*} $$

Question 5¶

Which of the following statements about local regression (e.g.,LOESS) is true?

  • (a) It is used primarily to predict categorical outcomes.
  • (b) It is less flexible compared to global regression models.
  • (c) It tends to underfit when the span is large.
  • (d) It assumes that the relationship between the predictors and the responses is linear throughout the domain of the predictors.

(c) is correct. The model cannot capture the trend of the data if the span is large then resulting in underfitting.

Question 6¶

What is the primary difference between cubic splines and natural cubic splines?

  • (a) Cubic splines are defined for each interval between data points, while natural cubic splines are only defined at the data points themselves.
  • (b) Cubic splines require the second derivative at the endpoints to be zero, whereas natural cubic splines do not have any restrictions on the derivatives.
  • (c) Natural cubic splines ensure that the second derivative at the endpoints of the spline is zero, while cubic splines do not have this restriction.
  • (d) Cubic splines are smoother and have higher continuity than natural cubic splines, which tend to have sharp turns at the data points.

(c) is correct.b

Question 7¶

This question uses the following variables from the boston data, which can be downloaded from canvas. We are interested in predicting the air quality variable nox.

(a) For this problem, we will estimate the conditional expectation of nox given indus (one predictor). We will consider three different estimators:

  • Linear regression with spline features and knots at {0,12,17,30}
  • Linear regression with polynomial features of degree 12
  • K-nearest-neighbors regression with 13 neighbors

Estimate the mean squared predictive error for each estimator using 4-fold cross-validation (remember to use the same splits for each estimator). Report the error for each of the estimators. Which estimator gives the lowest error?

Fit each estimator to the entire dataset and plot the three predicted curves against a scatterplot of indus vs nox in the data. Set alpha=0.1 in the scatterplot. (Otherwise, you will not be able to tell that there are many points that are “on top of each other”). Why might one choose to highlight the curve with the highest error when discussing air quality in a public presentation? A short explanation of one to three sentences will suffice.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures, SplineTransformer
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

X = bos['indus'].values.reshape(-1,1)
y = bos['nox']

knots = np.array([[0], [12], [17], [30]])
kf = KFold(n_splits=4, shuffle=True, random_state=42)

# transformer
spline = SplineTransformer(knots=knots)
poly = PolynomialFeatures(degree=12)

mse_spline = []
mse_poly = []
mse_knn = []

for i, (train_idx, test_idx) in enumerate(kf.split(X)):
    X_train = X[train_idx]
    X_test = X[test_idx]
    y_train = y[train_idx]
    y_test = y[test_idx]

    # linear regression with spline features
    X_train_spline = spline.fit_transform(X_train)
    X_test_spline = spline.fit_transform(X_test)
    m1 = LinearRegression()
    m1.fit(X_train_spline, y_train)
    y_pred_spline = m1.predict(X_test_spline)
    mse_spline.append(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred_spline))

    # linear regression with polynomial features 
    X_train_poly = poly.fit_transform(X_train)
    X_test_poly = poly.fit_transform(X_test)
    m2 = LinearRegression()
    m2.fit(X_train_poly, y_train)
    y_pred_poly = m2.predict(X_test_poly)
    mse_poly.append(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred_poly))

    # knn regression
    m3 = KNeighborsRegressor(n_neighbors=13)
    m3.fit(X_train, y_train)
    y_pred_knn = m3.predict(X_test)
    mse_knn.append(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred_knn))

result = {"mse_spline_avg": np.mean(mse_spline),
         "mse_poly_avg": np.mean(mse_poly),
         "mse_knn_avg": np.mean(mse_knn)}

print(result)

est = min(result.items(), key=lambda x: x[1])
print(f"{est[0]} has the lowest mse")

{'mse_spline_avg': np.float64(0.004560456505205405), 'mse_poly_avg': np.float64(0.003766081050145473), 'mse_knn_avg': np.float64(0.0032723282937460116)}
mse_knn_avg has the lowest mse

X_spline = spline.fit_transform(X)
X_poly = poly.fit_transform(X)

m1.fit(X_spline, y)
m2.fit(X_poly, y)
m3.fit(X, y)

X_plot = np.linspace(X.min(), X.max(), 300).reshape(-1, 1)

X_plot_spline = spline.transform(X_plot)
X_plot_poly = poly.transform(X_plot)

y_plot_spline = m1.predict(X_plot_spline)
y_plot_poly = m2.predict(X_plot_poly)
y_plot_knn = m3.predict(X_plot)

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
sns.scatterplot(x=X.flatten(), y=y, alpha=0.1, label="Observed", color="black")

plt.plot(X_plot, y_plot_spline, label="Spline Regression", color="blue")
plt.plot(X_plot, y_plot_poly, label="Polynomial Regression (deg=12)", color="red", linestyle="dashed")
plt.plot(X_plot, y_plot_knn, label="KNN Regression (k=13)", color="green", linestyle="dotted")

plt.xlabel("indus")
plt.ylabel("nox")
plt.legend()
plt.title("Regression Models for Predicting NOx Levels")
plt.show()

Highlighting the curve with the highest error can illustrate issues like overfitting or underfitting. It demonstrates the importance of proper model selection, feature representation, and robustness in predictive modeling. This helps convey why certain models fail to generalize well and the necessity of balancing bias and variance.

(b) Use pygam to predict nox from dis, indus, and rad. Treat each of these variables as continuous.

  • Use pygam to fit the data, considering different choices for the lam that controls the regularization strength. For each feature, consider four choices of regularization, $\lambda \in \{0.5,1,5,10\}$. (There will be $4^3 = 64$ fits in total.) Use pygam’s gridsearch method to identify the best choice. Report the best $\lambda$ value found.
  • Plot the partial dependence for each of the three features.
  • The feature rad indicates an index of accessibility to highways. How well do you think the estimated partial dependence for this feature represents the true relationship between rad and nox? Explain.
In [222]:
from pygam import LinearGAM, s, f
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV

# Define the feature matrix and response variable
X = bos[['dis', 'indus', 'rad']].values
y = bos['nox'].values

# Define the grid of lambda values
lam_values = [0.5, 1, 5, 10]
lam_grid = np.array(np.meshgrid(lam_values, lam_values, lam_values)).T.reshape(-1, 3)  # 4^3 = 64 combinations

# Fit the GAM model using grid search
gam = LinearGAM(s(0) + s(1) + s(2))
grid = gam.gridsearch(X, y, lam=lam_grid)

# Get the best lambda
best_lam = gam.lam
print(f"Best lambda values found: {best_lam}")

plt.figure(figsize=(15, 5))

for i, feature in enumerate(['dis', 'indus', 'rad']):
    plt.subplot(1, 3, i + 1)
    XX = grid.generate_X_grid(term=i)
    plt.plot(XX[:, i], grid.partial_dependence(term=i, X=XX))
    plt.plot(XX[:, i], grid.partial_dependence(term=i, X=XX, width=0.95)[1], c='r', ls='--')
    plt.title(f'{feature}')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The rad subplot shows an unclear relationship with nox, suggesting that rad may not have a strong effect. The wide confidence intervals indicate high uncertainty, likely due to limited data in some areas. If rad is correlated with other features or interacts with them, the partial dependence plot may not fully capture the true relationship.
